cases.title: The invoice that almost worked
cases.summary: An accounts assistant reports an overdue invoice. Decide what the email proves—and what it does not.
objectives: Compare sender identity with authentication results
Separate delivery, clicks, and credential exposure
cases.lesson: A display name is not an identity check. SPF authenticates the sending server for the envelope domain; DKIM validates a signature; DMARC checks alignment with the visible From domain. Authentication failure is a clue, not a verdict. Correlate the message, its destination, and user activity before claiming compromise.
cases.brief: You are covering the morning queue at fictional Harbour Services. At 09:14 UTC on 4 September, Mia in accounts forwards an invoice reminder she did not expect. The supplier usually sends invoices through an established portal. No response action has been taken.

evidence.title: Original email headers
evidence.body:
From: Harbour Supplier <billing@harbour-invoices.example>
Return-Path: <notice@bulk-mail.example>
Subject: FINAL NOTICE — invoice 8841
Authentication-Results: spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bulk-mail.example; dkim=none; dmarc=fail header.from=harbour-invoices.example
Delivery: delivered to mia@harbour.example

evidence.title: Message and URL analysis
evidence.body:
Message asks Mia to sign in to prevent a late fee.
Displayed link: Supplier invoice portal
Actual destination: hxxps://harbour-payments.example/login
Offline page capture: asks for Harbour email and password.
Approved supplier portal in vendor register: vendor-portal.example
Attachment count: 0

evidence.title: User report and activity
evidence.body:
Mia: 'I forwarded it without opening the link.'
Proxy search, 09:00–09:18: no requests to harbour-payments.example from Mia's managed laptop.
Identity search: no anomalous sign-ins during this window.
Coverage: managed laptop only; personal mobile activity is unavailable.
Mail search: same message delivered to two other accounts staff.

questions.prompt: What is the most defensible classification?
options: Confirmed account takeover
Likely credential phishing; compromise is not established
Benign because SPF passed
questions.explanation: E1 shows SPF passed for bulk-mail.example, not the visible sender. E2 shows a mismatched credential collection page. E3 does not establish a click or credential submission.

questions.prompt: Which evidence best limits your confidence about exposure?
options: There were no attachments
The subject uses urgent language
The proxy search covers only the managed laptop
questions.explanation: E3 explicitly excludes personal mobile visibility. A clean search within one data source cannot prove no interaction occurred anywhere.

questions.prompt: What should the authorised responder do first?
options: Preserve the message, quarantine matching deliveries, and check the other recipients for interaction
Disable every finance account immediately
Close the case because Mia reported no click
questions.explanation: Preserve evidence and reduce exposure to the known campaign while checking scope. Mass account disablement is unsupported; closure would ignore the other recipients.

cases.handover: Likely credential phishing delivered to three accounts staff at 09:11 UTC. E1–E2 show sender misalignment and an unapproved login destination. No managed-laptop interaction is visible for Mia; personal mobile activity and the two other recipients remain unverified. Ask the authorised mail responder to preserve and quarantine matching messages, then confirm interaction and identity activity for all recipients.
cases.reflection: What additional evidence would change this from an email exposure case into an identity incident?

cases.title: Two cities, one session
cases.summary: An impossible-travel alert looks urgent. Trace the network context before disrupting a user.
objectives: Document an explained detection without ignoring gaps
cases.lesson: An impossible-travel rule compares location and time. VPN exits, proxies, and mobile carriers can move the apparent location. Device, session, authentication method, network ownership, and user confirmation provide stronger context. A familiar device or successful MFA alone does not guarantee safety.
cases.brief: At 02:09 UTC, the identity platform flags Alex for sign-ins labelled Sydney and Singapore eight minutes apart. Alex is a service coordinator working remotely. The alert has not triggered containment.

evidence.title: Sign-in pair
evidence.body:
02:00 user=alex@harbour.example ip=192.0.2.24 city=Sydney device=HBR-LT-042 session=S-771 auth=FIDO2 result=success
02:08 user=alex@harbour.example ip=198.51.100.18 city=Singapore device=HBR-LT-042 session=S-771 auth=existing_session result=success
Device compliance: compliant in both events.
IP addresses are documentation placeholders; city labels are synthetic.

evidence.title: Network context
evidence.body:
198.51.100.18 is the documented Singapore exit for the company's remote-access provider in this exercise.
02:06 VPN connection: user=alex device=HBR-LT-042 exit=198.51.100.18
No new authentication factor or device was registered during the alert window.

evidence.title: Verification and follow-up
evidence.body:
Alex confirms starting the corporate VPN at 02:06 during a support call. Callback used the directory number, not contact details in an incoming message.
Audit review 01:30–02:25: expected ticketing access; no unusual downloads, mailbox rules, or privilege changes.
No visibility outside this review window.

questions.prompt: What does the combined evidence support?
options: An explained travel alert caused by the approved VPN
Confirmed stolen session because two countries appear
No need to investigate alerts with successful MFA
questions.explanation: E2 explains the change of apparent location, and E1 plus E3 corroborate the session and user activity. The conclusion rests on several sources, not MFA alone.

questions.prompt: Which correlation most directly explains the location change?
options: Alex works remotely
The VPN log matches the user, device, exit IP, and time
The second city is a common travel destination
questions.explanation: E2 links the specific sign-in change to an approved connection at 02:06. A general fact about remote work does not explain this event.

questions.prompt: How should you finish this investigation?
options: Suppress all alerts from Singapore
Revoke all sessions and state that credentials were stolen
Record the VPN explanation and reviewed window; propose narrowly scoped tuning for review
questions.explanation: Document the evidence and limits. Any tuning should require the verified network context and review, rather than excluding an entire location or treating all VPN traffic as safe.

cases.handover: Impossible-travel alert explained by an approved VPN connection at 02:06 UTC. E1–E2 correlate Alex, device HBR-LT-042, session S-771, and the documented exit. Known-number callback and audit review support expected activity through 02:25. Close as an explained detection with the review window recorded; submit narrowly scoped VPN-context tuning for review.
cases.reflection: Which new sign-in or audit event would make you reopen this case?

cases.title: PowerShell after the document
cases.summary: A document launches a script interpreter. Establish the process chain and contain the right asset.
objectives: Distinguish an attempted connection from successful execution
cases.lesson: A process name alone rarely proves intent. Parent-child relationships, command lines, file paths, network results, and prevention outcomes explain behaviour. A blocked request does not mean every earlier action was blocked. Preserve volatile evidence where feasible, and use approved containment procedures rather than improvising destructive cleanup.
cases.brief: Endpoint protection raises a high-confidence alert for HBR-LT-117, a finance laptop. You have authority to recommend isolation to the on-call responder, but you cannot execute actions on real endpoints from this lab.

evidence.title: Process timeline
evidence.body:
11:42:01 explorer.exe → WINWORD.EXE C:\Users\sam\Downloads\invoice.docm
11:42:05 WINWORD.EXE → powershell.exe -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden [script content redacted]
11:42:06 powershell.exe writes C:\Users\sam\AppData\Local\Temp\update.dat
User=sam@harbour.example host=HBR-LT-117
Training evidence only; no executable payload is provided.

evidence.title: Protection and network events
evidence.body:
11:42:07 outbound HTTPS request to update-cache.example blocked by proxy policy.
11:42:08 endpoint alert: suspicious Office child process; detection-only rule.
Host isolation: not active.
No later process telemetry available yet.
The file write in E1 preceded the network block.

evidence.title: Asset and scope
evidence.body:
HBR-LT-117: managed finance workstation; standard user; no safety-critical function.
Fleet search over last 24h: one matching Office-to-PowerShell chain.
The file hash has not yet been collected.
Responder available; user is on an established support call.

options: No execution occurred because the proxy blocked the request
Suspicious execution occurred; later payload activity is unknown
Confirmed fleet-wide ransomware
questions.explanation: E1 establishes script execution and a file write. E2 blocks one network request but leaves subsequent activity unknown. E3 does not show a fleet-wide outbreak.

questions.prompt: Which evidence should you preserve and obtain next?
options: Only the alert title
A screenshot of the user's desktop
Process details, the written file's hash, and follow-on endpoint telemetry
questions.explanation: The process chain, file identity, and subsequent activity allow the responder to determine scope and outcome. Do not execute the suspicious file to investigate it.

options: Ask the authorised responder to isolate HBR-LT-117 under the playbook and preserve evidence
Reimage immediately before collecting any evidence
Close the case as fully prevented
questions.explanation: The affected endpoint is known and suspicious execution is evidenced. Approved isolation limits further activity while allowing investigation; immediate reimaging can destroy useful evidence.

cases.handover: Escalate suspicious document-triggered execution on HBR-LT-117 at 11:42 UTC. E1 records WINWORD spawning PowerShell and a file write; E2 blocked a later request but the endpoint rule was detection-only. Only one matching host is currently known. Request authorised endpoint isolation, preserve process and file evidence, and collect follow-on telemetry before deciding eradication or recovery.
cases.reflection: How would your containment recommendation change if this host controlled a safety-critical process?

cases.title: The export nobody expected
cases.summary: A large customer export coincides with a new sharing link. Test the exfiltration hypothesis.
objectives: Separate data access from external transfer
Contain exposed access without overstating impact
cases.lesson: A large download may be legitimate, and an external link may create exposure without proving that anyone accessed it. Establish the sensitivity, actor, business purpose, sharing configuration, and access evidence separately. Record log gaps as unknowns. Involve the incident lead and privacy owner through the organisation's process when sensitive data may be exposed.
cases.brief: At 16:05 UTC, a data-loss rule flags a customer export by Jordan in operations. The duty lead asks whether customer data has left the organisation. Your answer needs to distinguish facts from a plausible but unproven hypothesis.

evidence.title: Data activity
evidence.body:
Actor: jordan@harbour.example
Action: export customer records; rows=4200; file=customers-september.csv
Fields: names, business email addresses, customer account references.
Destination: managed company workspace.
Historical export size: typically 100–300 records.

evidence.title: Sharing event
evidence.body:
File: customers-september.csv
Action: anonymous link created; permission=view/download; expiry=none
External link access audit: unavailable during 15:55–16:10 due to ingestion delay.
Link creation confirms exposure potential, not external access.
Anonymous sharing can be revoked by the workspace responder.

evidence.title: Business context
evidence.body:
Approved task: deduplicate customer records inside the managed workspace.
Manager confirms a full export was authorised for this task.
Anonymous sharing was not approved.
Jordan reports creating a link to share with a colleague and says it was not sent externally. This account is not independently verified.

questions.prompt: What can you tell the duty lead?
options: 4,200 records were definitely stolen
The export is authorised, so there is no security issue
An unauthorised anonymous link exposed the file; external access is currently unknown
questions.explanation: E3 supports the export's business purpose but not anonymous sharing. E2 establishes an exposure and a log gap, not confirmed external access.

questions.prompt: What evidence is most important to resolve the impact question?
options: Recovered link-access logs, recipients, and download events for the exposure window
Jordan's job title
The number of characters in the filename
questions.explanation: Access and download evidence, together with where the link was sent, help determine whether the potential exposure became an actual external disclosure. Missing logs must remain a stated limitation.

questions.prompt: What is the best immediate response?
options: Delete the file and its audit history
Have the authorised responder revoke anonymous access, preserve audit evidence, and involve the incident lead
Wait for all logs to arrive before limiting access
questions.explanation: Remove the known exposure without destroying evidence. The incident lead can coordinate the data owner's and privacy team's assessment while the access evidence is recovered.

cases.handover: An approved 4,200-record customer export was given an unapproved anonymous download link at 15:58 UTC. External access is unknown because of a log ingestion gap. Request immediate authorised revocation of anonymous access, preserve export/sharing events, and recover access logs and link recipients. Escalate the potential exposure to the incident lead for data-owner and privacy review; do not report confirmed theft.
cases.reflection: Write one sentence that communicates urgency without presenting the missing access logs as proof of safety or theft.

cases.title: A noisy night shift
cases.summary: A scheduled scanner triggers repeated failures. Explain the alert without creating a blind spot.
objectives: Correlate a detection with an approved change
Distinguish authorised activity from harmless activity
cases.lesson: A false positive deserves evidence, not a dismissive note. Verify the source asset, expected targets, time window, and observed behaviour against an approved task. Tuning should preserve detection of deviations and have an owner and review date. Never disable an entire detection just because one instance is explained.
cases.brief: The queue contains 87 failed-login alerts from 198.51.100.40 between 01:00 and 01:20 UTC. A colleague suggests adding the address to a permanent allowlist. Review the evidence first.

evidence.title: Authentication summary
evidence.body:
Window: 01:00–01:20 UTC
Source: 198.51.100.40
Targets: HBR-SRV-010 through HBR-SRV-019
Failures: 87; successes: 0
Account pattern: svc_scan
No observed targets outside this group in the supplied window.

evidence.title: Approved change
evidence.body:
Window: 01:00–01:30 UTC on 4 September
Scanner: HBR-SCAN-01 / 198.51.100.40
Target group: HBR-SRV-010 through HBR-SRV-019
Purpose: credentialed vulnerability assessment
Owner: infrastructure on-call
Change does not authorise other accounts or targets.

evidence.title: Scanner execution record
evidence.body:
Job J-442 started 01:00 and ended 01:20.
Target list matches CHG-204.
Credential validation failed for svc_scan after a recent password rotation.
Owner confirms the job and will repair the credential before the next approved run.
No production account lockouts recorded in the supplied window.

questions.prompt: What is the best current disposition?
options: Explained authorised scan with a credential configuration issue
Confirmed password spraying by an attacker
All future activity from this IP is trusted
questions.explanation: The source, targets, account, timing, and execution record agree with CHG-204. This explains this instance; it does not establish permanent trust.

questions.prompt: Which change would invalidate this explanation?
options: The scan finishes inside the approved window
The same source attempts a privileged account on an out-of-scope server
The owner repairs the scanner credential
questions.explanation: E2 does not authorise other accounts or targets. Such a deviation needs fresh investigation even if the source address is unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which tuning proposal preserves useful coverage?
options: Disable failed-login detection
Permanently suppress the source IP for all accounts
Match approved scanner, account, targets, and change window; assign an owner and expiry
questions.explanation: A scoped exception can reduce expected noise while retaining signals outside the authorised behaviour. Review and expiry prevent an old exception silently becoming permanent.

cases.handover: The 87 failures correlate with approved scanner job J-442 under CHG-204, including source, target group, account, and window. Credential rotation caused scanner authentication failures; no successes or lockouts are recorded in the supplied window. Close this detection as explained and assign credential repair to infrastructure. Any tuning must match the approved behaviour, retain deviation alerts, and expire for review.
cases.reflection: Why does ownership and expiry matter even when a tuning rule is carefully scoped?

cases.title: Leave a case someone can continue
cases.summary: A suspicious sign-in and mailbox rule arrive at shift change. Set priority, scope, and the next action.
objectives: Assign priority from the supplied impact rubric
Write a concise handover with facts, gaps, owner, and action
cases.lesson: A useful handover gives the next analyst a starting point: what happened, when, to which assets or users, what evidence supports the assessment, what has been done, what remains unknown, and who owns the next action. Here P1 means widespread or critical service impact requiring immediate coordination; P2 means credible compromise of a sensitive account needing urgent response; P3 means suspicious activity needing routine investigation. These are exercise-specific priorities, not a universal standard.
cases.brief: Your shift ends at 18:00 UTC. An executive assistant's account has a new external mail-forwarding rule after an unusual sign-in. The assistant handles executive travel and invoices. The authorised identity responder is available but needs your handover. Use the priority rubric in the lesson.

evidence.title: Identity timeline
evidence.body:
17:31 user=lee@harbour.example source=203.0.113.77 device=unmanaged session=S-990 result=success
17:30 MFA push approved after four denied prompts.
17:42 known-number callback: Lee denies the sign-in and says they accepted a prompt to stop repeated notifications.
No new factor registration observed.

evidence.title: Mailbox changes
evidence.body:
Actor=lee@harbour.example session=S-990
New rule: forward messages containing 'invoice' to archive@external-mail.example, then move original to Archive.
Rule enabled=true
No approved delegation or forwarding change exists.
Historical message-access and forwarding-delivery search: pending.

evidence.title: Scope and response state
evidence.body:
Known affected account: Lee only. No critical service outage.
Lee can still use the account. Sessions have NOT been revoked. Forwarding rule has NOT been disabled.
Identity responder: on-call duty analyst.
Preserved evidence: sign-in records, MFA events, and rule configuration.
Open questions: messages accessed/forwarded, other rules, other affected users.

questions.prompt: Which priority matches the supplied rubric?
options: P3 because only one account is known
P2: credible compromise of a sensitive account requiring urgent response
P1 because every suspicious login is a critical outage
questions.explanation: The user's denial, MFA fatigue, and session-linked forwarding rule support credible compromise of a sensitive account. No widespread or critical service impact is evidenced, so P2 matches this exercise's rubric.

questions.prompt: Which statement belongs in the factual handover?
options: All invoice emails were stolen
Containment is complete
Session S-990 created an unapproved forwarding rule; actual forwarding and access remain under investigation
questions.explanation: E1–E2 correlate the session and rule. E3 says containment is outstanding and message impact is unknown. A handover must not turn planned actions into completed ones.

questions.prompt: What should the incoming responder do next under the account-compromise playbook?
options: Revoke suspicious sessions, secure the account and MFA, disable the unauthorised rule, and investigate mail access while preserving evidence
Delete the mailbox and close the case
Wait until tomorrow because no outage is visible
questions.explanation: Contain the active identity and mail risks through authorised procedures, then determine impact and scope. Check that actions succeeded and maintain an owner for follow-up; a lack of outage does not make the compromise low priority.

cases.handover: P2 suspected account compromise: lee@harbour.example. At 17:31 UTC, unmanaged session S-990 followed repeated MFA prompts; Lee denies the sign-in. At 17:34 the same session created an unapproved external invoice-forwarding rule. Identity and rule evidence is preserved. As of 17:50 neither session revocation nor rule removal has occurred. The on-call identity responder owns urgent containment under the playbook, confirmation of success, and investigation of message access/forwarding, other rules, and related users. One account is known affected; data disclosure remains unconfirmed.
cases.reflection: Write your own handover before revealing the example. Include timing, scope, evidence, response state, unknowns, and an owner.
